corrected_draft.title: 2025 Law Retains CHIP Enrollment Protections While Narrowing Some Immigrant Eligibility
corrected_draft.description_short: The 2025 law retained several CHIP protections but separately narrowed Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for many lawful immigrants.
corrected_draft.description_medium: Georgetown’s post-enactment analysis says the July 4, 2025 reconciliation law retained separate-state CHIP protections against waiting periods, missed-premium lockouts, annual or lifetime limits, and coverage gaps during transitions. The law separately limits Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for many lawfully present immigrants beginning October 1, 2026. The original claim that states could restore the listed CHIP restrictions is incorrect.
corrected_draft.description_long: President Donald Trump signed the 2025 reconciliation law, P.L. 119-21, on July 4, 2025. Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families reviewed the enacted provisions and reports that several key protections for children in separate state CHIP programs remained in effect: states could not impose CHIP waiting periods, lock out children over missed premiums, or apply annual or lifetime dollar limits, and Medicaid and CHIP agencies still had to coordinate eligibility transitions. The same law contains separate changes to immigrant eligibility. The analysis says section 71109 removes Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for many lawfully present immigrants, including refugees and asylees, effective October 1, 2026, while retaining eligibility for specified groups such as green-card holders after five years and certain other categories. The held claim that the law restored waiting periods and lockouts is wrong. These distinct provisions should not be collapsed into a claim that all children’s coverage protections were removed.

The announcement drew criticism from some people who had expected broader disclosure, but this child should focus on the memo and its conclusions. children.title: Trump asks DOJ to investigate Epstein ties of Clinton and other political targets
children.description_short: Trump said he would ask the Justice Department to investigate Jeffrey Epstein's ties to Bill Clinton, JPMorgan and others.
children.description_medium: On November 14, 2025, Trump asked DOJ to investigate Epstein-related ties of Bill Clinton, Larry Summers, Reid Hoffman and JPMorgan; DOJ said it would comply and assigned Jay Clayton. Reuters said no credible evidence linked the named individuals to Epstein’s trafficking. Reuters said the request followed House Oversight’s release of Epstein documents.
children.description_long: On November 14, 2025, President Trump publicly asked the Justice Department to investigate Jeffrey Epstein’s connections with former President Bill Clinton, former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers, investor Reid Hoffman and JPMorgan. Reuters reported that Attorney General Pam Bondi said Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton would lead the investigation. The request came two days after the House Oversight Committee released a large set of Epstein-related documents and amid renewed political attention to Trump’s own past association with Epstein. Reuters reported that no credible evidence had surfaced linking Clinton, Summers or Hoffman to Epstein’s sex trafficking; the named individuals denied wrongdoing or described their contacts. This entry should report the request and DOJ’s stated response without suggesting that the investigation found crimes or that the targets had been accused of sexual offenses. It is separate from the July DOJ/FBI memorandum and the July defamation lawsuit over the birthday-note story.

children.description_short: The CFPB attempted to dismiss roughly 1,400 to 1,500 employees in April, potentially eliminating about 90% of the agency's workforce.

children.description_long: A federal judge temporarily halted the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s planned mass layoffs in April 2025. Reuters, in a report republished by Inc., said the bureau intended to dismiss roughly 1,400 to 1,500 employees, a reduction approaching 90% of its workforce. The court order prevented the dismissals from proceeding while the legal challenge continued. The source therefore documents a proposed reduction and judicial intervention, not that the entire workforce was actually terminated. The court proceedings also bear on whether the agency could continue work, so the proposal should not be presented as a completed shutdown. This April episode followed February work stoppages and preceded separate reports that some CFPB functions resumed. It should be recorded independently with the court’s temporary status made clear; the original broad claim that all enforcement matters were dropped requires a separate case-by-case review of agency and court records.
